Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Alejandro Rivera was driving his sedan through a heavy rain when a delivery truck ran the red light at the intersection. The collision was a sudden, violent compression of space. He cannot reconstruct the sequence of events into a coherent account; the memory remains a jumble of physical sensations and broken fragments. When it surfaces, he hears the sharp hiss of the deployed airbag and the wet crack of his own rib cage under the dashboard. Each time those sounds return in his mind, a heavy shame settles over him, as if the wreck had been a direct reflection of his moral character. He became certain that he would never experience his former emotional landscape again, that his capacity for ordinary feeling was permanently severed. He also arrived at the quiet conviction that he was utterly powerless to prevent calamity, and that the accident had occurred precisely because of the kind of man he was. Alongside these beliefs, a current of strong negative emotions—fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame—frequently rose without warning, sharp and unbidden. In the months that followed, these beliefs and sensations coexisted with a heightened vigilance that colored his days. Alejandro began scanning for doorways and fire exits the moment he stepped into any new space. At the rehearsal studio where he taught contemporary dance, the narrow staging doors and mirrored walls became rooms he had to map before breathing easily. When his wife, Elena, or a choreographer reached out to correct his stance without warning, his body would jump with alarm, shoulders tightening, breath catching. He tried hard to push the trauma from his thoughts whenever it intruded, forcing his attention toward the metronome or the music cue. When the suppression failed, he deliberately let his awareness drift, stepping out of his body until the present felt distant and flat. He also began delaying sleep, staying awake until very late in the night, convincing himself that if he simply remained upright, he would not have to face what waited in the dark. The daily weight of these experiences accumulated in quiet, concrete ways. He stopped teaching the lifts and partner work, telling his students he was preserving his joints, though the reality was that standing near them meant risking an unexpected touch. He found himself sitting in his parked car long after the building emptied, hands resting on the wheel, eyes tracking the garage doors even though he was already outside. The distance between him and Elena grew not from arguments, but from his steady retreat into wakefulness and mental quieting. He watched his students’ faces harden slightly when he canceled sessions, and he noted how his own voice had lost its usual cadence, replaced by a flat, measured tone. At sixty-two, the exhaustion of maintaining this constant separation finally outweighed his usual reserve. He noticed how the shame on recall was bleeding into his conversations with Elena, how the helplessness made even running errands feel like navigating unpredictable terrain, how the blank spaces in his memory were no longer manageable silences but persistent gaps in his own identity. He scheduled an intake because the quiet had become too heavy to carry alone. What he hoped for was not a dramatic reversal, but a chance to stop fighting his own nervous system, to feel the floor beneath his feet without flinching, and to believe, however tentatively, that he was not fundamentally broken by the night the metal gave way.
